passage: At home in Malda for the holidays, Tanvir spread five semesters of marksheets on the floor of his room, next to the calendar his cousin Nitin had printed. "Something's not random," he muttered. He put a finger on each dip. Semester two: the dip matched the month he'd helped run the village youth club's football tournament. Semester four: the month he'd taken extra shifts at his uncle's phone repair shop during Durga Puja. Semester five, the failed one: he'd been building a website for the local school, late every night, right through exams. "It's not that I can't study," he told Nitin. "It's that I say yes to one more thing just when exams come." He marked the next two exam windows in red on the calendar. Above them he wrote: "No tournaments. No shop. No new projects." Then, smaller: "After exams, yes to everything."

qa.q: What did Tanvir build in semester five?
qa.a: A website for the local school.

qa.q: How does Tanvir feel on spotting the pattern?
qa.a: Tanvir feels relieved and a little surprised, seeing the dips came from extra commitments, not inability.

qa.q: What else could Tanvir do before exam windows?
qa.a: Tanvir could tell the youth club and his uncle the exam dates in advance, so saying no is easier when requests come.

qa.q: How might Tanvir's uncle see the new plan?
qa.a: His uncle may miss the extra help at festival time but would likely understand once he knows the exam dates.

grounding: Shows a student looking at past terms, noticing marks fall whenever a side project or part-time task overlaps with exams, and planning to pause them then.

passage: In his student flat in Kraków, Marek opened a spreadsheet with every grade since first year. Bao, his flatmate, leaned on the doorframe with a mug. "You're actually doing it?" "You told me to." He had added a column: what else was happening that month. The pattern was hard to miss. His lowest marks, including the two failed exams last term, came in months when his band had gigs or he'd picked up extra shifts at the bike shop. In quiet months he'd scored well, some of his best. "So you're not bad at statistics," Bao said. "You're bad at statistics when you're playing three gigs a week." Marek laughed, then went quiet. He opened his calendar and blocked out the two weeks before each exam period in grey. "No gigs, no extra shifts. I'll tell the band now, not in panic week."

qa.q: What did Marek add to the spreadsheet?
qa.a: A column for what else was happening that month.

qa.q: How did Marek feel when Bao summed it up?
qa.a: Marek laughed, then went quiet, likely feeling both relieved and a bit sobered by the clear pattern.

qa.q: What else could Marek do with the pattern?
qa.a: Marek could check next term's gig schedule against the exam dates now, and swap any clashing shifts early.

qa.q: How might the band see Marek's decision?
qa.a: The band may be disappointed to lose him in exam weeks, but hearing early gives them time to plan around it.

grounding: Illustrates a student finding that past marks dropped whenever gigs or extra shifts overlapped exams, and blocking those weeks off in future.
